tier_reason: First-party numbers from the repo's own runner (run_benchmarks.ps1 / run_benchmarks.sh over benchmarks/bench_*.lua) against native Lua 5.5 on a named CPU (Ryzen 7 5800X; macOS snapshot on Apple M4), but the rustc version and the native Lua build/compiler/flags used for the snapshots are not stated, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Windows snapshot (docs/benchmarks/windows.md, Ryzen 7 5800X), luars throughput as % of native Lua 5.5: arithmetic 111, control flow 87, locals 132, functions 92, closures 80, multiple returns 78, tables 92, table library 118, iterators 93, math 98, metatables 78, OOP 92, coroutines 152, errors 103 (9 of 14 scripts below parity). macOS snapshot (docs/benchmarks/macos.md, Apple M4, contributed by @sniper00): arithmetic 136, control flow 143, locals 143, functions 119, closures 99, multiple returns 105, tables 141, table library 301, iterators 123, math 140, metatables 121, OOP 109, coroutines 113, errors 120 (13 of 14 above parity); string scripts about 99 and 120. README: Linux runs are often 20% to 40% slower than native Lua on broad coverage while winning a subset (no Linux numbers in the repo).
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X (Windows snapshot); Apple M4 (macOS snapshot)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: luars: cargo build --release with the default release profile (no custom [profile.release] in the workspace Cargo.toml); rustc version not stated. Native Lua build used for the snapshots not stated (the CI workflow builds lua-5.5.0 with make linux / make macosx and CMake Release on Windows, but CI numbers are not in the repo).
corrections.workload: Script-level Lua microbenchmarks in benchmarks/ (bench_arithmetic.lua through bench_errors.lua) run by run_benchmarks.ps1 (Windows) or run_benchmarks.sh (macOS); each value is luars throughput divided by native Lua 5.5 throughput times 100. The runners execute 18 scripts but the snapshot charts show 14 (bench_tailcall, bench_gc, bench_strings and bench_string_lib are left out of the Windows chart).
corrections.caveats: Mixed result: on Windows 9 of 14 scripts are slower than native Lua 5.5, and the README says Linux runs are often 20-40% slower (no maintained Linux snapshot, only a CI workflow whose output is not in the repo); the faster macOS snapshot (13 of 14 above parity, table library 301%) was contributed by a third party on an Apple M4 with no build details. The author attributes the Windows coroutine win (152%) partly to native Lua's longjmp cost on Windows. The luars interpreter binary installs mimalloc as its global allocator while native Lua uses the system malloc, which may account for part of the table/GC-heavy wins. rustc version and native Lua build flags for the snapshots are not stated; tailcall, GC and string scripts are omitted from the Windows chart (strings because of timer resolution). The README states the project was written through AI-assisted programming.

notes: Numbers on windows.md match the record exactly; the record missed docs/benchmarks/macos.md, which does carry numbers (Apple M4, mostly faster). Shortcomings to record: mixed/not faster on Windows and Linux, unequal allocators (mimalloc vs system malloc), native Lua build unstated, AI-assisted code (now confirmed in the README, not snippet only).

tier_reason: Vendor numbers (Pydantic sells the commercial Full Monty) from public code (scripts/startup_performance.py) on a named CPU (Apple M3 Max) with the release profile in Cargo.toml, but the rustc version is not stated and the comparison is sandbox startup latency, not interpreter speed against CPython; vendor rule keeps it at C.

corrections.baseline: CPython-based sandboxes (WASI/wasmtime with precompiled CPython 3.14.7, local Docker python:3.14-alpine, Pyodide in Deno via mcp-run-python, a Daytona sandboxing service) and starlark-rust; the same page also times plain unsandboxed CPython (in-process eval/exec and a python -c subprocess). No CPython execution-throughput claim in the repo docs.
corrections.hardware: Apple M3 Max, 96 GB, macOS 26.5.2 (driven from CPython 3.14.7); Full Monty rows measured in linux/arm64 Docker containers on one machine
corrections.compiler_and_flags: monty worker binary built with the workspace release profile (lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, strip = true); rustc version not stated (rust-version 1.96 minimum)
corrections.workload: scripts/startup_performance.py: time to get a fresh sandbox and run 1 + 1, and an agent run of 10 REPL commands (AGENT_BLOCKS) against an existing sandbox; sandboxes without a persistent interpreter replay commands 1..n for command n.
corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/index.md and docs/alternatives.md: OSS Monty new sandbox 0.80 ms (checkout from an already-open pool; 0.77 ms median of 20 after 1 s idle; 5 ms when the pool is created) vs WASI/wasmtime 16 ms, local Docker 195 ms, sandboxing service 1500 ms, Pyodide in Deno 2700 ms; 10-command agent run 0.40 ms vs 180 ms, 700 ms, 400 ms and 35 ms; combined 1.20 ms vs 200 ms, 900 ms, 1900 ms and 2700 ms. Plain unsandboxed CPython on the same page: eval about 0.1 ms and ten exec calls 0.3 ms (faster than Monty), python -c subprocess about 30 ms and ten replayed subprocesses about 180 ms. starlark-rust first parse+eval 1.3 ms.
corrections.caveats: The claim is sandbox startup latency against container, Wasm and hosted sandboxes, not interpreter throughput against CPython, so it does not meet the category baselines; against plain in-process CPython (0.1 ms eval, 0.3 ms for ten exec calls) Monty is slower. Monty's number is a checkout from an already-created pool (median of 20) while the others start from nothing with a single sample, and Monty was re-measured on 2026-09-24 while most other rows date from 2026-09-03. Vendor documentation: Pydantic sells Full Monty. Monty implements a Python subset (no class inheritance, limited stdlib, no third-party packages). A monty-bench crate (Criterion) compares Monty with CPython but publishes no numbers in the repo; a search snippet of project material said runtime speed is generally between 5x faster and 5x slower than CPython (snippet only). pydantic.dev docs site blocked here; the same text is in docs/ in the repo.

notes: Numbers match docs/index.md; docs/alternatives.md carries the methodology (script path, M3 Max, CPython 3.14.7, sample counts), so it is the better benchmark_url. Shortcomings to record: startup-latency comparison against sandboxes rather than CPython speed, slower than in-process CPython exec, pooled-vs-cold asymmetry, vendor evidence, Python subset.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the third-party go-quickjs/go-js-engines-benchmark harness (arewefastyet-v8v7/main.go with engines/paserati.go, plus factorial/) is public, pins Paserati v0.9.13, goja and fastschema/qjs v0.0.6 in go.mod, runs with go run . on Go 1.27.0, and names the CPU (Apple M5 Max). The README's own hyperfine table (bench/hyperfine.sh) alone would be C (no hardware or Go version).

corrections.baseline: goja (dop251/goja, pure-Go JavaScript engine) and QuickJS ports usable from Go: QJS (fastschema/qjs, QuickJS compiled to WebAssembly) and ModerncQuickJS (ccgo-translated QuickJS) in the third-party shootout; the README's own hyperfine table uses a 'qjs' QuickJS runner binary of unstated origin. Neither native QuickJS nor V8 is measured.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Third-party shootout: Go 1.27.0, go run . with default flags, Paserati type checking disabled. README hyperfine run: Go version and build flags not stated; paserati invoked with --no-typecheck.
corrections.hardware: Apple M5 Max, 128 GiB RAM, macOS ARM64 (third-party shootout, results collected 2026-10-05); README hyperfine hardware not stated
corrections.workload: Third-party shootout: V8 v7 suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes; one full run per engine) and recursive factorial(10) one million times (5 runs, alternating order). README: bench/bench.js (xorshift arithmetic and array microbenchmark) and bench/objects.js (object/inline-cache microbenchmark) timed with hyperfine via bench/hyperfine.sh (warmup 3, at least 20 runs).
corrections.claimed_speedup: Third-party shootout (Apple M5 Max, Go 1.27.0): V8 v7 score Paserati 1125 vs goja 751, ModerncQuickJS 787, QJS 761 (about 1.5x goja, derived from page data), duration 36.567 s vs 51.188 s, 48.447 s, 52.086 s; factorial average 515.824 ms vs goja 703.527 ms (1.36x, derived from page data), ModerncQuickJS 653.106 ms, QJS 592.033 ms. GoQuickJS, a pure-Go QuickJS-NG port, is far faster than Paserati (score 3912, factorial 213.392 ms; Paserati is 2.42x slower on factorial). README hyperfine: bench/bench.js 3.924 s vs goja 5.207 s (1.33x) vs QJS 4.945 s (1.26x); bench/objects.js 6.169 s vs goja 7.015 s (1.14x) vs QJS 8.135 s (1.32x).
corrections.caveats: Beats goja and the Wasm/ccgo QuickJS builds, but not the fastest Go JavaScript engine: GoQuickJS scores 3.5x higher on V8 v7 and is 2.4x faster on factorial in the same third-party shootout; native QuickJS and V8 (the category baseline) are not measured. The shootout is maintained by the go-quickjs organization (a competing engine), forked from ngocphuongnb/go-js-engines-benchmark, has 0 stars, and runs the V8 suite once per engine; it tested Paserati v0.9.13 with type checking disabled. The README's own numbers are two first-party microbenchmarks with no hardware or Go version, run with --no-typecheck, and the identity of its 'qjs' binary is unstated. The author says it prioritizes correctness over speed and that almost all code was written by AI models under direction. The V8-suite page linked from the README is on a blocked github.io site.

notes: README numbers match exactly; a public third-party harness with Go version, run command and CPU supports the win over goja and QJS, so tier upgraded C to A. Shortcomings to record: far slower than GoQuickJS (pure-Go QuickJS-NG port), no V8 or native QuickJS baseline (off the category baselines; QuickJS is an embedded-scripting baseline), first-party README table lacks methodology, AI-written code. Could not verify the record's statement that the shootout author also wrote QJS; replaced with the fork lineage.
